top_choice_rationale: P001 (Pakes, Berry, Levinsohn, B005) does best on what the work changed about what can be credibly known and on validation through use. The Berry-Levinsohn-Pakes framework made substitution patterns, markups and merger effects estimable from market data with endogenous prices, and about three decades of use in merger review, antitrust, regulation and applied work have tested it. The credit core is one jointly authored estimator, so a citation limited to demand and competition in differentiated-product markets matches the three names without implying credit for the dynamic strand (Benkard, Levin) or the earlier market-power tradition (Bresnahan, Reiss). The main reservations are that it rewards a method rather than a headline finding, and that estimates are sensitive to instruments and functional form, so the citation should not suggest settled magnitudes. I do not count the ten supporters as evidence of merit. I rank P002 (Autor, Hanson, Dorn) second because its design-based evidence is credible and its trio is cleanly attributed, but the debates over persistence, magnitude and shift-share identification leave it less mature. P000 is last because P001 and P002 each reach the bar on achievement, attribution and citation scope. I have not independently verified the claims about prior prizes or replication records.
recusal_note: None apparent from profile. No co-authorship with Pakes, Berry, Levinsohn, Autor, Hanson or Dorn is recorded. I overlapped institutionally at Stockholm University with the IIES macro group, which is not a co-authorship. Bertil Holmlund is my long-standing co-author and also a frequent co-author of Randi Hjalmarsson, who proposes P002. That is a committee-relationship tie, not a candidate tie. My own work and the 2021 presentation speech are in the design-based tradition, which may bias me toward credible-identification criteria. I disclose these ties without adjudicating them.
